module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 34

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/34](https://www.erdosproblems.com/34)
- [Er77c] Erdős, Paul, *Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. III*. Number theory day
  (Proc. Conf., Rockefeller Univ., New York, 1976) (1977), 43-72.
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [He86] Hegyvári, N., *On consecutive sums in sequences*. Acta Math. Hungar. (1986),
  193--200.
- [Ko15] Konieczny, J., *On consecutive sums in permutations*. arXiv:1504.07156 (2015).
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos34

open scoped BigOperators

/-- The set of consecutive sums of a permutation `p` of `{1,…,n}`, where position `k` holds the
value `p k + 1`: the sums `∑_{u ≤ k ≤ v} (p k + 1)`. -/
def consecutiveSums (n : ℕ) (p : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : Finset ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter (fun x : Fin n × Fin n => x.1 ≤ x.2)).image
    (fun x => ∑ k ∈ Finset.Icc x.1 x.2, ((p k : ℕ) + 1))

/--
For any permutation $\pi\in S_n$ of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ let $S(\pi)$ count the number of distinct consecutive sums, that is, sums of the shape $\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}\pi(i)$. Is it true that
$$
S(\pi) = o(n^2)
$$
for all $\pi\in S_n$?

Hegyvári [He86] gave a counterexample.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11,
  formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos34.lean"]
theorem erdos_34 : answer(False) ↔
    ∀ c : ℝ, 0 < c → ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n ≥ N, ∀ p : Equiv.Perm (Fin n),
      ((consecutiveSums n p).card : ℝ) < c * (n : ℝ) ^ 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos34

reformulations.difference: The source asks whether "S(π) = o(n²) for all π ∈ S_n". Read literally, that is an asymptotic statement about every sequence of permutations π_n ∈ S_n. The Lean right-hand side is instead the uniform ε–N statement `∀ c > 0, ∃ N, ∀ n ≥ N, ∀ p : Equiv.Perm (Fin n), card < c * n^2`. It quantifies over all permutations for each n and uses a strict `<`. The answer is fixed as `answer(False)`, so the theorem asserts the negation of this uniform statement.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Take the per-sequence reading. (⇒) The uniform bound gives the bound for any sequence π_n. (⇐) Pick π_n to be a maximiser of S over the finite nonempty S_n. The o(n²) bound for this one sequence with constant c/2 gives, for n ≥ max N 1, S(p) ≤ S(π_n) ≤ (c/2)n² < c n² for every p. The same argument, taking c/2 and n ≥ 1, shows that strict `<` and non-strict `≤` agree. It also shows equivalence with max_π S(π) = o(n²), which is the phrasing in the OEIS A389241 comment. The uniform form is literally Konieczny's Question 1 (arXiv:1504.07156): 'for any ε > 0 there exists n₀ such that for any n ≥ n₀ and any a ∈ Sym([n]), |S(a)| ≤ εn²'. The answer is 'no' (Konieczny's Prop. 1.1 gives |S(a)| ≥ n²/4 for every n; Hegyvári gives (1/18+o(1))n²), so `answer(False)` has the correct polarity. I proved all three equivalences in Lean without sorry: RHS ↔ the `≤ ε n²` form, RHS ↔ `∀ π : (n : ℕ) → Equiv.Perm (Fin n), (fun n => (card : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun n => (n:ℝ)^2)`, and RHS ↔ `(max over Finset.univ.sup) =o[atTop] n^2`.

review.notes:
I found no misformalization. Lean checks run in /workspace/review:
(1) `#eval` of `consecutiveSums` on small inputs. Identity on [3] gives {1,2,3,5,6}; (1,3,2) gives all of {1,…,6}; n = 0 gives the empty set.
(2) On every permutation of Fin n for n ≤ 6, `consecutiveSums` agrees with an independent list-based count.
(3) The identity values 1, 3, 5, 9, 12, 16, 21, 27 match OEIS A234813. The max over permutations, 0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 13, 19, 25, 32, matches OEIS A389241.
(4) Konieczny's permutation 1, n, 2, n−1, … gives ≥ n²/4 sums for n < 30.
(5) I proved the right-hand side equivalent to Konieczny's ε–n₀ form, to the per-sequence `IsLittleO` form and to the max form. `answer(False) ↔ RHS` unfolds to `¬ RHS`.
(6) The external proof's `perm_consecutive_sums` elaborates to the same term as `consecutiveSums` (`rfl`). Its `¬ erdos_34` closes the file's statement in one line, so the `formal_proof` record is accurate.

Boundary case n = 0: the RHS's strict inequality fails there (0 < 0 is false), but N is existential, and ¬RHS still needs n ≥ N for every N, so this trivialises neither direction.

Status (`research solved`, `answer(False)`) matches both erdosproblems.com and the teorth database ('disproved (Lean)').

References: the module docstring's citations match the OEIS and Konieczny bibliographies. [Er77c] is the Rockefeller 'Problems and results on combinatorial number theory III' (pp. 43–72), which is consistent with erdosproblems' [Er77c, p.71]. Konieczny cites the 1977 Manitoba paper instead; OEIS lists both. I did not read the original Erdős texts ([Er77c] p.71, [ErGr80] p.58) directly. For the wording I relied on erdosproblems.com, Konieczny's Question 1 and the OEIS A389241 comment, which all agree.

The source also discusses f(n) = max S, the random-permutation asymptotic and the minimum g(n). None of these is formalized, and their absence is not a defect.
